reference.source: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery / Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine
clinicalPearls: A non-atherosclerotic segmental inflammatory occlusive disease of small and medium arteries and veins of the distal limbs
Overwhelmingly affects young tobacco users, typically men under forty, with a strong and causal relationship to smoking
Presents with distal ischaemia including digital pain, claudication of the foot or hand, cold sensitivity, ulceration, and gangrene of the toes or fingers
Migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and Raynaud phenomenon are recognised associated features
Both upper and lower limbs may be involved, distinguishing it from typical atherosclerotic peripheral disease
Diagnosis is clinical and by exclusion, supported by angiographic findings of distal segmental occlusions with corkscrew collaterals and absence of proximal atheroma or an embolic source
Complete and permanent tobacco cessation is the single most effective intervention and can halt progression and prevent amputation
Standard revascularisation is often not feasible because of the distal small-vessel pattern, so wound care and abstinence are central
reference.pathophysiology: Buerger disease (thromboangiitis obliterans) is a segmental non-atherosclerotic vasculitis affecting small and medium arteries and veins of the extremities. There is an inflammatory, highly cellular thrombus with relative sparing of the vessel wall and internal elastic lamina, distinguishing it histologically from atherosclerosis and other vasculitides. Tobacco exposure is central to pathogenesis, likely through an immune-mediated and endothelial mechanism, and continued use drives progression. Occlusion of distal vessels produces critical ischaemia of the digits with limited collateral compensation.
additionalDifferentials: Embolic occlusion from a cardiac or proximal arterial source
Connective tissue disease with digital ischaemia (e.g. scleroderma)
additionalInvestigations: Angiography demonstrating distal segmental occlusions with corkscrew collaterals and absence of proximal atheroma
Echocardiography and proximal arterial imaging to exclude an embolic source
Autoimmune and vasculitis serology to exclude systemic vasculitis and connective tissue disease
Tobacco use assessment including confirmatory testing when abstinence is claimed
redFlags: Rest pain, ulceration, or digital gangrene indicating critical ischaemia and threatened tissue loss
Rapidly progressive digital necrosis, particularly with continued smoking
Ascending infection of an ischaemic digit
Involvement of multiple limbs signalling extensive disease
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is closely tied to smoking behaviour: complete cessation usually arrests the disease and greatly reduces amputation risk, whereas continued tobacco use commonly leads to recurrent ischaemia and progressive tissue loss. Life expectancy is generally near normal, but limb and digit loss is the major morbidity.
pitfalls: Diagnosing atherosclerotic disease in a young smoker and missing thromboangiitis obliterans
Underemphasising that continued smoking, including any tobacco or nicotine exposure, drives progression
Pursuing revascularisation where the distal small-vessel pattern makes it unsuitable
Failing to exclude an embolic source or systemic vasculitis before settling on the diagnosis
management: Achieve complete and permanent tobacco cessation as the single decisive intervention that arrests the disease and greatly reduces amputation risk, supported by structured cessation programmes
Protect the extremities and provide meticulous wound care to treat and prevent digital ulceration and secondary infection, avoiding cold and trauma
Manage ischaemic rest pain with analgesia and use an intravenous prostacyclin analogue such as iloprost for critical ischaemia and ulceration
Treat migratory superficial thrombophlebitis and associated Raynaud phenomenon symptomatically
Consider sympathectomy or spinal cord stimulation for refractory rest pain, since the distal segmental disease is rarely amenable to arterial reconstruction
Reserve amputation for intractable pain, gangrene or uncontrolled infection, keeping it as distal as possible
Refer to a multidisciplinary vascular, pain and podiatry service and reinforce abstinence at every review
